h1: Home Power Planner: Free Electricity Calculators
author: ali-ahmad
answer: The Home Power Planner sizes a home running {{out.running_w|int}} W from one appliance list: an inverter of {{out.inverter_buy}}, about {{out.battery_kwh|1}} kWh of battery for {{in.backup_hours|1}} hours and {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW of solar. The best fit is {{out.decision}}, saving about {{out.decision_saving_rs|rs}} a month with your power cuts.
key_facts: The planner carries one appliance list through the whole chain: running load, inverter, battery, solar, net billing and generator, each with the formula of its own calculator, so the sizes never contradict each other.

The decision step compares on-grid solar, hybrid solar with a battery, a UPS or petrol generator, and on-grid solar with that UPS or generator, for the same home: price range, backup time, bill saving and running cost a month, and the net cost over the years you choose. It recommends the setup with the lowest net cost that gives the backup you asked for and fits your budget.

Inverter size = running watts × {{d.margin|2}}, raised if needed so the solar array is at most {{d.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} times it; battery Ah = backup watts × hours ÷ (bank volts × usable depth of discharge × inverter efficiency); solar kW = daily units ÷ city yield (the grid covers the moments when everything runs at once), with net billing counting, and the setups pricing, the array only up to the sanctioned load; generator kVA = the larger of running × {{d.margin|2}} and the starting peak, ÷ {{d.pf_generator|1}}.

Default values (inverter efficiency {{d.inverter_eff_ups|pct}} UPS and {{d.inverter_eff_hybrid|pct}} hybrid, usable battery capacity {{d.dod_lead_acid|pct}} tubular and {{d.dod_lifepo4|pct}} lithium, power factor {{d.pf_mixed|2}}) are listed on the methodology page and editable in each calculator.

Pakistan tariff slabs, peak sun hours by city and appliance wattages live in dated data files; the net-billing buyback rate is NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}} under the {{data.tariff.net_billing.regulation}}, and stays editable.
Results are planning estimates, not an official bill or an engineer's design; wiring and solar work must be confirmed by a licensed electrician.

sections.h2: What the planner does, step by step
p: Step one adds up the appliances you tick: the watts that run at once and the units they use in a day. Step two sizes the inverter for that running load with a safety margin, and step four can raise it so the inverter accepts the solar array. Step three sizes the battery for only the load you want to keep on during loadshedding, for the hours you choose. Step four sizes the solar array for your daily units and your city's sun. Step five splits a month's solar between what you use while the sun is up and what you export, and compares the bill with and without net billing: the energy charge alone, and the whole bill with fixed charge, surcharges and GST. Step six sizes a generator for the whole list, in case you want one for long outages.

Step seven is the decision. It prices four setups with the dated price data behind the solar price and backup cost calculators: on-grid solar (the array above, installed), hybrid solar (the same array with the battery bank and a hybrid inverter), a UPS or petrol generator for the backup load only, and on-grid solar together with that UPS or generator. Each gets a price range, the backup it gives, the monthly bill saving or running cost, and the net cost over the years you pick: price plus battery replacements plus running cost minus bill saving. The cheapest net setup that gives your backup hours is recommended; with a budget, a setup counts when the low end of its price range fits it (leave the budget blank for no limit). When the runner-up's range of net cost overlaps the pick's, the result says it is a close call, so get quotes for both. On-grid solar earns only while the grid is on: the planner spreads your power cut hours evenly over the day, so a hybrid also exports only while the grid is on, and a generator is credited with the grid units it supplies.

What this comparison leaves out: installation of the UPS or generator (their prices are equipment only), the inverter's own idle draw on the battery (the battery pages count {{a.ups-idle.running_w|int}} W for a home UPS; a large hybrid inverter can draw two or three times that, so allow a little more battery), battery losses on solar self-use, inverter replacement, the daytime solar the hybrid battery stores, the leftover value of a battery replaced near the end of the period, and price changes over the years (every figure is in today's rupees). Power cuts are spread evenly over the day, so cuts that fall mostly at midday cost on-grid solar more than shown. To [[N7|compare backup costs in detail]], the UPS vs solar vs generator calculator prices the same backup on equipment and running cost alone and leaves out the bill saving, so its cheapest pick can differ from the one here. To [[C1|size a generator for motors]] and the rest of your own list, with each starting surge shown, use the generator size calculator.
Every step is a calculator on this site. Open any of them from the task cards below to change its assumptions, see worked examples and read the formula.

Start with the task, not the jargon. If the lights go out during loadshedding, start with the battery and UPS tools. If the bill is the problem, start with the bill calculators and the AC consumption tool. If you are planning solar, add up your home load first, then size the system.

Each result page ends with a Next step link to the tool that naturally follows, so a battery backup time leads to inverter sizing, a home load leads to solar sizing, and a wire size leads to the breaker to pair with it.

sections.h2: Why the numbers can be trusted
p: The calculators share one engine with one set of formulas and one set of constants. The same formula produces the live result, the worked examples, the reference tables and the FAQ answers on every page, so every number comes from one engine; where two pages show a different bill for the same units, each one names its own inputs, such as the sanctioned load and the FPA.

The formulas follow standard electrical practice (IEC and NEPRA performance standards for a {{d.v_1ph|int}} V, {{d.v_3ph|int}} V three-phase, fifty hertz supply). Assumptions that depend on judgement are marked and editable, and a review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress.

faq.q: Can I save or share my plan?
faq.a: Yes. Press the plan button, then use Save as PDF to print or keep the page, WhatsApp to send the sizes and a link to your installer, or copy the link: it carries your appliance list, so whoever opens it sees the same plan.

faq.q: Which is better for my home: solar, hybrid solar or a UPS?
faq.a: It depends on the backup you need, your bill and your budget, so the planner compares four setups for your own list. For the example home, on-grid solar costs {{out.ongrid_low_rs|rs}} to {{out.ongrid_high_rs|rs}} and saves {{out.ongrid_saving_rs|rs}} a month (only while the grid is on) but gives no backup, because an on-grid inverter switches off in a power cut. Hybrid solar adds {{out.hybrid_battery}} and a grid-tie hybrid inverter that can still export, and costs {{out.hybrid_low_rs|rs}} to {{out.hybrid_high_rs|rs}} (the hybrid inverter's extra cost over an on-grid one is added only where our price lists show one; the result says which). A {{out.standby_option}} costs {{out.standby_low_rs|rs}} to {{out.standby_high_rs|rs}} and costs about {{out.standby_running_rs|rs}} a month to run (a UPS through the bill, a generator in petrol and oil, though a generator also takes the backup units it supplies off the bill). On-grid solar with that {{out.standby_option}} costs {{out.combo_low_rs|rs}} to {{out.combo_high_rs|rs}} and gives backup and most of the bill saving (a UPS recharge comes off it). Over {{out.years}} years the recommended setup is {{out.decision}}. Prices are ranges from dated data and the middle price decides, with a close call flagged when the ranges overlap; solar prices include installation, UPS and generator prices are equipment only, and a battery replaced near the end of the period is counted in full.

faq.q: How does the planner work out the saving on the whole bill?
faq.a: It prices {{out.monthly_units|int}} units the way the bill calculator does: energy charge, fixed charge for your sanctioned load, FC surcharge and GST, for {{out.full_before_rs|rs}}. With solar you import {{out.import_units|int}} units, billed the same way at {{out.full_import_rs|rs}}, and the {{out.export_units|int}} exported units earn {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}}, set against that bill, leaving {{out.full_after_rs|rs}}. The whole-bill saving, with no power cuts, is {{out.full_saving_rs|rs}}, of which {{out.saving_rs|rs}} is energy charge; the rest is the lower fixed charge band, surcharge and GST. QTA and FPA change month to month and are left at zero here, and the planner assumes GST is charged on the imported units before the export credit, the cautious reading. The buyback rate is NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}; it stays editable because NEPRA sets it again each year. Agreements signed before {{data.tariff.net_billing.existing_cutoff}} stay on the old net-metering terms until they expire, unless the system is enlarged, which moves it to net billing.
Yes. Every tool runs in your browser, needs no sign-up and stores nothing about you. You can share a result by copying the page link after you press Calculate.

faq.q: Do the tools work outside Pakistan?
faq.a: Yes. The defaults are set for Pakistan ({{d.v_1ph|int}} V single phase, rupees, local tariff slabs), and the converters, battery, solar and wiring tools let you switch to {{d.v_1ph_us|int}} V or enter your own voltage and prices.

They are planning estimates built on typical values. Real backup time, bills and solar output depend on battery age, weather, the exact appliance and the tariff of the month, so expect the real number to land near the estimate, not exactly on it.

faq.q: Who writes and checks the tools?
faq.a: Wattlyst is written by its founder, Ali Ahmad, with formulas documented on the methodology page. Technical review by a PEC-registered electrical engineer is in progress and will be named on each page once complete.

fields.label: Appliances you run (edit the list)
fields.hint: Watts and hours fill in from our appliance data; change any value to match your home.

fields.label: City (for sun hours)

fields.name: sanctioned_kw
fields.label: Sanctioned load
fields.hint: The kW printed on your electricity bill. Below {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} keeps the flat tariff and caps net billing; at {{d.tou_threshold_kw|int}} kW or more use the [[F13|ToU bill calculator]].

fields.name: backup_w
fields.label: Load to keep on during loadshedding
fields.hint: Fans, lights, Wi-Fi and TV are a few hundred watts; an inverter AC adds over a thousand.

fields.name: backup_hours
fields.label: Backup hours wanted
fields.hint: Hours of power cuts a day you want covered from the battery (or UPS or generator); the planner spreads them evenly over the day.

fields.name: budget_rs
fields.label: Budget
fields.hint: The most you want to spend now. Leave it blank to compare without a limit.

fields.name: years
fields.label: Years to compare
fields.hint: The net cost adds the price, battery replacements, running cost and bill saving over this many years.

fields.name: buyback_rs
fields.label: Net-billing buyback rate
fields.hint: Rs per exported unit: NEPRA's national average energy purchase price for {{data.tariff.net_billing.buyback_period}}. Change it only if your DISCO bills a revised rate.

fields.name: day_share
fields.label: Share of use while the sun is up
fields.hint: How much of the day's electricity you use between sunrise and sunset. Half is typical for a home.

fields.name: margin
fields.label: Sizing margin
fields.hint: Inverter and generator are sized at the running load times this margin.

how: Your list runs {{out.running_w|int}} W at once ({{out.peak_w|int}} W when the biggest motor starts) and uses {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units a day, {{out.monthly_units|int}} a month. Battery: {{in.backup_w}} W × {{in.backup_hours|1}} h = {{out.backup_kwh|2}} kWh ÷ ({{out.battery_v}} V × {{out.battery_dod|pct}} usable × {{d.inverter_eff_hybrid|pct}} inverter) = {{out.battery_ah|up}} Ah. Solar: energy {{out.daily_kwh|1}} kWh ÷ {{out.city_yield|1}} kWh per kW per day = {{out.solar_kw_energy|2}} kW; with the grid connected the array is sized by energy, because the grid supplies the rest whenever the {{out.running_w|int}} W running load is more than the panels give, so {{out.solar_kw|2}} kW needs {{out.panels|int}} panels of {{out.panel_w|int}} W = {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW making about {{out.monthly_solar_kwh|int}} units a month. Inverter: the larger of {{out.running_w|int}} W × {{in.margin|2}} = {{out.inverter_kw_load|2}} kW and the {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW solar array ÷ {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} = {{out.inverter_kw_array|2}} kW (an inverter takes panels up to about {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} times its rating, so it must be at least the array divided by that), so at least {{out.inverter_kw|up1}} kW: the inverter to buy is {{out.inverter_buy}}. Net billing counts an array up to your {{out.sanctioned_kw|1}} kW sanctioned load: {{out.net_billing_panels|int}} panels, {{out.net_billing_kw|2}} kW, about {{out.net_billing_solar_kwh|int}} units a month; the setups below are priced at this array. You use {{out.self_used_units|int}} of those units yourself, export {{out.export_units|int}} at {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} and import {{out.import_units|int}}; energy charge {{out.bill_before_rs|rs}} before solar, {{out.bill_after_rs|rs}} after, saving {{out.saving_rs|rs}} a month on the energy charge alone. Whole bill (fixed charge, FC surcharge, GST {{out.gst_pct|int}}%): {{out.full_before_rs|rs}} before, {{out.full_import_rs|rs}} for the imported units, less {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} export credit, leaves {{out.full_after_rs|rs}} to pay ({{out.full_carry_forward_rs|rs}} credit carried to next month), saving {{out.full_saving_rs|rs}} a month. Generator for the whole list: {{out.generator_kva|1}} kVA, next standard size {{out.generator_pick_kva|1}} kVA. Decision over {{out.years}} years, net = price + battery replacements + every month of those years × (running cost − bill saving), in today's rupees. Power cuts take {{in.backup_hours|1}} hours a day, spread evenly over the day, so on-grid solar works {{out.grid_share|pct}} of the time and a hybrid exports only then; a generator's petrol is set against the grid units it supplies. {{out.decision_text}}
how_ur: Aap ki list ek waqt mein {{out.running_w|int}} W chalti hai (sab se bara motor start hone par {{out.peak_w|int}} W) aur roz {{out.daily_kwh|1}} units, mahine ke {{out.monthly_units|int}} units lagti hai. Battery: {{in.backup_w}} W × {{in.backup_hours|1}} h = {{out.backup_kwh|2}} kWh ÷ ({{out.battery_v}} V × {{out.battery_dod|pct}} qabil-e-istemal × {{d.inverter_eff_hybrid|pct}} inverter) = {{out.battery_ah|up}} Ah. Solar: energy {{out.daily_kwh|1}} kWh ÷ {{out.city_yield|1}} kWh fi kW roz = {{out.solar_kw_energy|2}} kW; grid saath ho to array energy se banta hai, kyun ke jab {{out.running_w|int}} W ka load panels se zyada ho to baqi grid deta hai, is liye {{out.solar_kw|2}} kW, yani {{out.panel_w|int}} W ke {{out.panels|int}} panels = {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW, mahine ke taqreeban {{out.monthly_solar_kwh|int}} units. Inverter: {{out.running_w|int}} W × {{in.margin|2}} = {{out.inverter_kw_load|2}} kW aur {{out.installed_kw|2}} kW solar array ÷ {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} = {{out.inverter_kw_array|2}} kW mein jo bara ho (inverter apni rating se taqreeban {{out.dc_ac_ratio_max|1}} guna tak panels le sakta hai, is liye array ko is se taqseem kar ke kam az kam itna inverter chahiye), yani kam az kam {{out.inverter_kw|up1}} kW: lene wala inverter {{out.inverter_buy}}. Net billing mein array aap ke {{out.sanctioned_kw|1}} kW sanctioned load tak gina jata hai: {{out.net_billing_panels|int}} panels, {{out.net_billing_kw|2}} kW, mahine ke taqreeban {{out.net_billing_solar_kwh|int}} units; neeche ke setups isi array ki qeemat par hain. In mein se {{out.self_used_units|int}} units khud istemal, {{out.export_units|int}} export {{out.buyback_rs|rs2}} par, {{out.import_units|int}} import; solar se pehle energy charge {{out.bill_before_rs|rs}}, baad mein {{out.bill_after_rs|rs}}, sirf energy charge par bachat {{out.saving_rs|rs}} mahana. Poora bill (fixed charge, FC surcharge, GST {{out.gst_pct|int}}%): pehle {{out.full_before_rs|rs}}, import units ka bill {{out.full_import_rs|rs}}, export credit {{out.export_credit_rs|rs}} minha kar ke baad mein {{out.full_after_rs|rs}} dena hai ({{out.full_carry_forward_rs|rs}} credit agle mahine), mahana bachat {{out.full_saving_rs|rs}}. Poori list ke liye generator: {{out.generator_kva|1}} kVA, agla standard size {{out.generator_pick_kva|1}} kVA. {{out.years}} saal ka faisla, kul = qeemat + battery badalna + un saalon ka har mahina × (kharcha − bill ki bachat), aaj ke rupay mein. Bijli {{in.backup_hours|1}} ghante band rehti hai, din bhar barabar baant kar, is liye on-grid solar {{out.grid_share|pct}} waqt chalta hai aur hybrid sirf tab export karta hai; generator ke petrol mein se woh grid units minha hote hain jo woh deta hai. {{out.decision_text}}
